claim: Processing of incoming sensory stimulation triggers an increase of cerebral perfusion and blood oxygenation (neurovascular response).
source: Processing of incoming sensory stimulation triggers an increase of cerebral perfusion and blood oxygenation (neurovascular response) as well as an alteration of the metabolic neurochemical profile (neurometabolic response).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience, supported by extensive literature and general scientific knowledge.

claim: Processing of incoming sensory stimulation triggers an alteration of the metabolic neurochemical profile (neurometabolic response).
source: Processing of incoming sensory stimulation triggers an increase of cerebral perfusion and blood oxygenation (neurovascular response) as well as an alteration of the metabolic neurochemical profile (neurometabolic response).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience, supported by extensive literature and general scientific knowledge.

claim: Perceived and unperceived isoluminant chromatic flickering stimuli designed to have similar neurovascular responses as measured by BOLD-fMRI have markedly different neurometabolic responses as measured by 1H-fMRS in human primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Here, we show in human primary visual cortex (V1) that perceived and unperceived isoluminant chromatic flickering stimuli designed to have similar neurovascular responses as measured by blood oxygenation level-dependent functional magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD-fMRI) have markedly different neurometabolic responses as measured by proton functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-fMRS).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from BOLD-fMRI and 1H-fMRS measurements.

claim: A significant regional buildup of lactate occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived.
source: In particular, a significant regional buildup of lactate, an index of aerobic glycolysis, and glutamate, an index of malate–aspartate shuttle, occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived, without any relation with other behavioral or physiological variables.
evidence: This is supported by 1H-fMRS measurements showing lactate increase during perceived flickering (PF) but not unperceived flickering (UF).

claim: Lactate is an index of aerobic glycolysis.
source: In particular, a significant regional buildup of lactate, an index of aerobic glycolysis, and glutamate, an index of malate–aspartate shuttle, occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived, without any relation with other behavioral or physiological variables.
evidence: This is based on established metabolic knowledge and cited literature in the manuscript.

claim: A significant regional buildup of glutamate occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived.
source: In particular, a significant regional buildup of lactate, an index of aerobic glycolysis, and glutamate, an index of malate–aspartate shuttle, occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived, without any relation with other behavioral or physiological variables.
evidence: This is supported by 1H-fMRS measurements showing glutamate increase during perceived flickering (PF) but not unperceived flickering (UF).

claim: Glutamate is an index of malate–aspartate shuttle.
source: In particular, a significant regional buildup of lactate, an index of aerobic glycolysis, and glutamate, an index of malate–aspartate shuttle, occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived, without any relation with other behavioral or physiological variables.
evidence: This is based on metabolic modeling and cited literature in the manuscript.

claim: The metabolic changes in V1 during perceived flickering occurred without any relation with other behavioral or physiological variables.
source: In particular, a significant regional buildup of lactate, an index of aerobic glycolysis, and glutamate, an index of malate–aspartate shuttle, occurred in V1 only when the flickering was perceived, without any relation with other behavioral or physiological variables.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of pupillometry, gaze displacement, and task performance data showing no differences across conditions.

claim: The BOLD-fMRI signal in V1 was insensitive to flickering perception by design.
source: Whereas the BOLD-fMRI signal in V1, a proxy for input to V1, was insensitive to flickering perception by design, the BOLD-fMRI signal in secondary visual areas was larger during perceived than unperceived flickering, indicating increased output from V1.
evidence: This is a consequence of the experimental design where stimulus contrast was adjusted to match BOLD responses in V1 for both conditions.

claim: The BOLD-fMRI signal in V1 is a proxy for input to V1.
source: Whereas the BOLD-fMRI signal in V1, a proxy for input to V1, was insensitive to flickering perception by design, the BOLD-fMRI signal in secondary visual areas was larger during perceived than unperceived flickering, indicating increased output from V1.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of BOLD signal and its relationship to neural activity, supported by citations.

claim: The BOLD-fMRI signal in secondary visual areas was larger during perceived than unperceived flickering.
source: Whereas the BOLD-fMRI signal in V1, a proxy for input to V1, was insensitive to flickering perception by design, the BOLD-fMRI signal in secondary visual areas was larger during perceived than unperceived flickering, indicating increased output from V1.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing differential activation in secondary visual areas (Brodmann Areas 18 and 19) between PF and UF conditions.

claim: Larger BOLD-fMRI signal in secondary visual areas during perceived flickering indicates increased output from V1.
source: Whereas the BOLD-fMRI signal in V1, a proxy for input to V1, was insensitive to flickering perception by design, the BOLD-fMRI signal in secondary visual areas was larger during perceived than unperceived flickering, indicating increased output from V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known connectivity between V1 and secondary visual areas.

claim: The upregulation of energy metabolism induced by visual stimulation depends on the type of information processing taking place in V1.
source: These results demonstrate that the upregulation of energy metabolism induced by visual stimulation depends on the type of information processing taking place in V1, and that 1H-fMRS provides unique information about local input/output balance that is not measured by BOLD-fMRI.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential metabolic responses despite similar BOLD responses.

claim: 1H-fMRS provides unique information about local input/output balance that is not measured by BOLD-fMRI.
source: These results demonstrate that the upregulation of energy metabolism induced by visual stimulation depends on the type of information processing taking place in V1, and that 1H-fMRS provides unique information about local input/output balance that is not measured by BOLD-fMRI.
evidence: This is concluded from the dissociation between BOLD and metabolic responses observed in the study.

claim: Sensory stimulation is associated with a substantial increase of regional functional hyperemia (i.e., cerebral blood flow, CBF) in the brain.
source: In the brain, sensory stimulation is associated with a substantial increase of regional functional hyperemia (i.e., cerebral blood flow, CBF) as well as energy metabolism of glucose, the main cerebral energy substrate (Siesjo, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siesjo, 1978.

claim: Sensory stimulation is associated with an increase in energy metabolism of glucose in the brain.
source: In the brain, sensory stimulation is associated with a substantial increase of regional functional hyperemia (i.e., cerebral blood flow, CBF) as well as energy metabolism of glucose, the main cerebral energy substrate (Siesjo, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siesjo, 1978.

claim: Glucose is the main cerebral energy substrate.
source: In the brain, sensory stimulation is associated with a substantial increase of regional functional hyperemia (i.e., cerebral blood flow, CBF) as well as energy metabolism of glucose, the main cerebral energy substrate (Siesjo, 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience, supported by citation.

claim: The metabolic response to stimulation includes an oxidative component, as measured by the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2).
source: The metabolic response to stimulation includes an oxidative component, as measured by the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2), and a nonoxidative component, as reflected by lactate accumulation (Mangia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mangia et al., 2009.

claim: The metabolic response to stimulation includes a nonoxidative component, as reflected by lactate accumulation.
source: The metabolic response to stimulation includes an oxidative component, as measured by the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2), and a nonoxidative component, as reflected by lactate accumulation (Mangia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mangia et al., 2009.

claim: Cortical lactate levels increase during visual stimulation.
source: Cortical lactate levels have been shown to increase during visual stimulation, simultaneously to the acceleration of the malate–aspartate shuttle (MAS), a process termed aerobic glycolysis (i.e., lactate production independent of oxygen availability) (Bednařík et al., 2015; Bednařík et al., 2018; Boillat et al., 2020; Fernandes et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012; Mangia et al., 2007a; Schaller et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The malate–aspartate shuttle (MAS) accelerates during visual stimulation.
source: Cortical lactate levels have been shown to increase during visual stimulation, simultaneously to the acceleration of the malate–aspartate shuttle (MAS), a process termed aerobic glycolysis (i.e., lactate production independent of oxygen availability) (Bednařík et al., 2015; Bednařík et al., 2018; Boillat et al., 2020; Fernandes et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012; Mangia et al., 2007a; Schaller et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis is lactate production independent of oxygen availability.
source: Cortical lactate levels have been shown to increase during visual stimulation, simultaneously to the acceleration of the malate–aspartate shuttle (MAS), a process termed aerobic glycolysis (i.e., lactate production independent of oxygen availability) (Bednařík et al., 2015; Bednařík et al., 2018; Boillat et al., 2020; Fernandes et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012; Mangia et al., 2007a; Schaller et al., 2013; Schaller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text, supported by citations.

claim: The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying the upregulation of glycolytic metabolism of glucose are still largely unknown.
source: Despite intense research, the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying the upregulation of glycolytic metabolism of glucose are still largely unknown (Dienel, 2019a).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: The impact of information processing on the metabolic response of the cerebral cortex to sensory stimulation has not been fully investigated.
source: Most importantly, the impact of information processing to the metabolic response of the cerebral cortex to sensory stimulation has not been fully investigated thus far.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Nothing is known about the modulatory effect exerted by the perception of different stimuli on regional brain energy metabolism.
source: In particular, nothing is known about the modulatory effect exerted by the perception of different stimuli on regional brain energy metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Sensory perception is thought to rely on the complex interplay of neural circuits that process information in a cortical layer- and area-mediated manner involving thalamocortical, intracortical, corticocortical, and corticothalamic feedforward/feedback loops.
source: Sensory perception is thought to rely on the complex interplay of neural circuits that process information in a cortical layer- and area-mediated manner involving thalamocortical, intracortical, corticocortical, and corticothalamic feedforward/feedback loops (D'Souza and Burkhalter, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to D'Souza and Burkhalter, 2017.

claim: Sensory stimuli transduced by sensory organs reach specific thalamic nuclei that relay information to primary sensory cortices.
source: Sensory stimuli transduced by sensory organs reach specific thalamic nuclei that relay information to primary sensory cortices, which in turn filter and eventually transmit information to secondary sensory areas (Crick and Koch, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crick and Koch, 1995.

claim: Primary sensory cortices filter and eventually transmit information to secondary sensory areas.
source: Sensory stimuli transduced by sensory organs reach specific thalamic nuclei that relay information to primary sensory cortices, which in turn filter and eventually transmit information to secondary sensory areas (Crick and Koch, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crick and Koch, 1995.

claim: The thalamic lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) mediates visual stimuli with temporal frequencies at least up to 90 Hz to the layer IV of V1.
source: The thalamic lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) mediates visual stimuli with temporal frequencies at least up to 90 Hz to the layer IV of V1 (Gur and Snodderly, 1997; Herrmann, 2001; Norcia et al., 2015; Pastor et al., 2003; Regan, 1989; Vialatte et al., 2010), which in turn relays to output layers II/III and V where temporal filtering occurs (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that visual perception requires the activation of visual areas downstream V1 (i.e., secondary visual areas).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Layer IV of V1 relays to output layers II/III and V where temporal filtering occurs.
source: The thalamic lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) mediates visual stimuli with temporal frequencies at least up to 90 Hz to the layer IV of V1 (Gur and Snodderly, 1997; Herrmann, 2001; Norcia et al., 2015; Pastor et al., 2003; Regan, 1989; Vialatte et al., 2010), which in turn relays to output layers II/III and V where temporal filtering occurs (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that visual perception requires the activation of visual areas downstream V1 (i.e., secondary visual areas).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013.

claim: Visual perception requires the activation of visual areas downstream V1 (i.e., secondary visual areas).
source: The thalamic lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) mediates visual stimuli with temporal frequencies at least up to 90 Hz to the layer IV of V1 (Gur and Snodderly, 1997; Herrmann, 2001; Norcia et al., 2015; Pastor et al., 2003; Regan, 1989; Vialatte et al., 2010), which in turn relays to output layers II/III and V where temporal filtering occurs (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013), consistent with the notion that visual perception requires the activation of visual areas downstream V1 (i.e., secondary visual areas).
evidence: This is stated as a notion consistent with the cited evidence about temporal filtering.

claim: Invisible visual flickering is able to activate V1 even without any perceptual effects.
source: In agreement with these arguments, it has been repeatedly reported that invisible visual flickering is still able to activate V1 even without any perceptual effects (Alais et al., 2016), as revealed by in vivo electrophysiology in nonhuman primates (Gur and Snodderly, 1997) as well as behavioral evidence (Lorenceau, 1987) and blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) (Jiang et al., 2007) in humans.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in nonhuman primates and humans.

claim: High (30 Hz) frequency visual stimulation selectively suppresses multiunit activity (MUA) in cat V1 as compared to low frequency (4 Hz) visual stimulation.
source: High (30 Hz) frequency visual stimulation has been found to selectively suppress multiunit activity (MUA) in cat V1 as compared to low frequency (4 Hz) visual stimulation (Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007.

claim: Local field potentials and tissue oxygen response are preserved at both high (30 Hz) and low (4 Hz) frequency visual stimulation.
source: Importantly, local field potentials and tissue oxygen response, which directly contribute to the generation of the BOLD signals (Logothetis et al., 2001), were preserved at both frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007 (implied from context) and Logothetis et al., 2001.

claim: Local field potentials and tissue oxygen response directly contribute to the generation of the BOLD signals.
source: Importantly, local field potentials and tissue oxygen response, which directly contribute to the generation of the BOLD signals (Logothetis et al., 2001), were preserved at both frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Logothetis et al., 2001.

claim: The critical flicker fusion (CFF) threshold for rod-mediated vision is approximately 15 Hz.
source: Specifically, we examined the functional and metabolic responses of the primary visual cortex (V1) to perceived or unperceived isoluminant chromatic flickering stimulation obtained by using temporal frequency either below (7.5 Hz; PF, perceived flickering) or above (30 Hz; UF, unperceived flickering) the critical flicker fusion (CFF) threshold of ~15 Hz for rod-mediated vision (Hecht and Shlaer, 1936).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hecht and Shlaer, 1936.

claim: The local input–output balance between neuronal synaptic/spiking activity is a primary determinant in the upregulation of aerobic glycolysis.
source: Based on experimental evidence and metabolic modeling, we have previously proposed that the local input–output balance between neuronal synaptic/spiking (or subthreshold/suprathreshold) activity is a primary determinant in the upregulation of aerobic glycolysis (DiNuzzo and Giove, 2012; DiNuzzo et al., 2011; DiNuzzo and Nedergaard, 2017).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The loss of visual perception is accompanied by fundamental changes in the metabolic responses of human V1.
source: We thus hypothesized that the loss of visual perception is accompanied by fundamental changes in the metabolic responses of human V1.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, which is tested with experimental data.

claim: The green/red brightness ratio for achieving perceptual isoluminance was 71.9% ± 1.2% (range 70.1–73.5%) across subjects.
source: To achieve perceptual isoluminance between green and red color (necessary for the UF condition), we adjusted the brightness of the green color for each individual subject, which was remarkably similar across subjects (green/red brightness ratio 71.9% ± 1.2%, range 70.1–73.5%) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: 100% of the subjects confirmed that their perception of the 30 Hz frequency stimulus steadiness was equivalent to the resting condition.
source: After this procedure, 100% of the subjects confirmed that their perception of the 30 Hz frequency stimulus steadiness was equivalent to the resting condition.
evidence: This is behavioral data from the study confirming the effectiveness of the UF condition.

claim: Subjects were unable to distinguish the 30 Hz red-green flickering checkerboard from a color-matched static yellow checkerboard.
source: Specifically, the perception of the steady yellow color versus the 30 Hz red-green flickering was indistinguishable, as assessed by asking the subjects to guess the origin of the stimulus for 10 consecutive trials (average of correct responses 52% ± 16%, not different from chance level, p = 0.62).
evidence: This is behavioral data from the study confirming subjects could not perceive the 30 Hz flickering.

claim: All subjects reported to distinctly perceive the green and red color when the checkerboard was flickering at 7.5 Hz.
source: All subjects reported to distinctly perceive the green and red color when the checkerboard was flickering at 7.5 Hz.
evidence: This is behavioral data from the study confirming the effectiveness of the PF condition.

claim: None of the subjects perceived the intrinsic flickering of the screen due to the refresh rate (60 Hz).
source: None of the subjects perceived the intrinsic flickering of the screen due to the refresh rate (60 Hz).
evidence: This is behavioral data from the study.

claim: All subjects maintained gaze on the fixation cross within 0.2–0.3° during all fMRI epochs.
source: All subjects maintained gaze on the fixation cross within 0.2–0.3° during all fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) epochs, with no difference in average gaze location between the different stimulations (one-way analysis of variance [ANOVA], p = 0.96 and p = 0.38, for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and p = 0.29 and p = 0.19 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is eye-tracking data from the study, also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in average gaze location between the different stimulations during fMRI and 1H-fMRS epochs.
source: All subjects maintained gaze on the fixation cross within 0.2–0.3° during all fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) epochs, with no difference in average gaze location between the different stimulations (one-way analysis of variance [ANOVA], p = 0.96 and p = 0.38, for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and p = 0.29 and p = 0.19 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of eye-tracking data from the study.

claim: Pupil diameter was fairly stable at around 6.5–7 mm on average during all fMRI and 1H-fMRS epochs.
source: Pupil diameter, an index of the noradrenergic tone (DiNuzzo et al., 2019), was fairly stable at around 6.5–7 mm on average during all fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) epochs (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.99 and p = 0.98, for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and p = 0.98 and p = 0.96 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) across conditions (see also Video 1), indicating that the modulation of perception by noradrenaline (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) was minimal in our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is pupillometry data from the study, also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pupil diameter is an index of the noradrenergic tone.
source: Pupil diameter, an index of the noradrenergic tone (DiNuzzo et al., 2019), was fairly stable at around 6.5–7 mm on average during all fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) epochs (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.99 and p = 0.98, for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and p = 0.98 and p = 0.96 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) across conditions (see also Video 1), indicating that the modulation of perception by noradrenaline (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) was minimal in our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DiNuzzo et al., 2019.

claim: The modulation of perception by noradrenaline was minimal in the experimental conditions.
source: Pupil diameter, an index of the noradrenergic tone (DiNuzzo et al., 2019), was fairly stable at around 6.5–7 mm on average during all fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) epochs (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.99 and p = 0.98, for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and p = 0.98 and p = 0.96 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) across conditions (see also Video 1), indicating that the modulation of perception by noradrenaline (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2018) was minimal in our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the stable pupil diameter data and supported by citation.

claim: The hit/miss ratio for the cross rotation task during the stimulation protocol was essentially 1.0 for the entire duration of the experiment.
source: The hit/miss ratio for the cross rotation task during the stimulation protocol was essentially 1.0, as expected due to the simplicity of the task, for the entire duration of the experiment.
evidence: This is task performance data from the study.

claim: The delay of the response was not statistically different for rest, PF and UF epochs during fMRI and 1H-fMRS.
source: In particular, the delay of the response was not statistically different (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.09 and p = 0.77 for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and p = 0.35 and p = 0.51 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) for rest, PF and UF epochs (ranging, on average, between 360 and 460 ms), both during fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), confirming high and similar levels of subject's attention across conditions.
evidence: This is task performance data from the study, also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was not significant correlation between mean pupil diameter and task performance during fMRI and 1H-fMRS.
source: There was not significant correlation between mean pupil diameter (two-tailed t-test, qFDR = 1 and qFDR >0.16 for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and qFDR >0.14 and qFDR >0.88 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) or gaze displacement (two-tailed t-test, qFDR = 1 and qFDR >0.59 for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and qFDR >0.13 and qFDR = 1 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) and task performance during both fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the relationship between physiological measures and task performance, also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: There was not significant correlation between gaze displacement and task performance during fMRI and 1H-fMRS.
source: There was not significant correlation between mean pupil diameter (two-tailed t-test, qFDR = 1 and qFDR >0.16 for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and qFDR >0.14 and qFDR >0.88 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) or gaze displacement (two-tailed t-test, qFDR = 1 and qFDR >0.59 for fMRI runs 1 and 2, respectively, and qFDR >0.13 and qFDR = 1 for 1H-fMRS runs 1 and 2, respectively) and task performance during both fMRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and 1H-fMRS (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the relationship between physiological measures and task performance, also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: In-scanner head motion during fMRI scans was minimal and not significantly different for all subjects across epochs.
source: Finally, in-scanner head motion during fMRI scans was minimal and not significantly different for all subjects across epochs (mean framewise displacement 0.25 ± 0.12 mm for rest, 0.24 ± 0.14 mm for PF, 0.23 ± 0.08 mm for UF; one-way ANOVA, p = 0.77).
evidence: This is motion analysis data from the study.

claim: Behavioral and physiological variables associated with attentional load were maintained at considerably constant levels in all subjects.
source: Overall, behavioral and physiological variables associated with attentional load were maintained at considerably constant levels in all subjects.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the pupillometry, gaze, and task performance data.

claim: The stimulation contrast for the 7.5 Hz condition was reduced to 75% relative to the 30 Hz condition to achieve the same BOLD response in V1 during PF and UF.
source: To achieve the same BOLD response in V1 during PF and UF, we reduced the stimulation contrast for the 7.5 Hz condition to 75% relative to the 30 Hz condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an experimental design choice, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The average BOLD time course did not differ between PF and UF.
source: As expected, we found that the average BOLD time course (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.42), onset time (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.93) and time-to-peak (paired sample t-test, p = 0.29) did not differ between PF and UF (Figure 1A, C and D).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 1A, C and D.

claim: The BOLD onset time did not differ between PF and UF.
source: As expected, we found that the average BOLD time course (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.42), onset time (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.93) and time-to-peak (paired sample t-test, p = 0.29) did not differ between PF and UF (Figure 1A, C and D).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 1A, C and D.

claim: The BOLD time-to-peak did not differ between PF and UF.
source: As expected, we found that the average BOLD time course (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.42), onset time (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.93) and time-to-peak (paired sample t-test, p = 0.29) did not differ between PF and UF (Figure 1A, C and D).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 1A, C and D.

claim: The BOLD change in the subject-matched spectroscopic volume-of-interest (VOI) was not different between PF (0.44% ± 0.30%) and UF (0.41% ± 0.25%).
source: Similarly, the BOLD change in the subject-matched spectroscopic volume-of-interest (VOI; on average consisting of 47% ± 9% of BA17, 21% ± 12% of BA18, and 16% ± 9% of BA19), was not different (0.44% ± 0.30% for PF vs 0.41% ± 0.25% for UF, paired sample t-test, p = 0.71) between the two conditions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bayesian analysis indicated moderate evidence for the absence of a difference in BOLD change between PF and UF conditions in the spectroscopic VOI.
source: Bayesian analysis indicated moderate evidence for the absence of a difference between conditions (paired sample Bayesian t-test, BF01 = 3.2).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of fMRI data from the study.

claim: The fMRI activations to PF and UF both peaked in V1 and distinctly spanned bilaterally in secondary visual areas.
source: The fMRI activations to PF and UF both peaked in V1 and distinctly spanned bilaterally in secondary visual areas ((Figure 2A, B), one-sample t-test, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected at cluster level, q < 0.05, voxel level p < 0.001).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The main effect of PF appeared in the lateral occipital cortices, but not in V1.
source: To better characterize the effect of the two different stimulations, we estimated the main effect of the flickering frequency. The main effect of PF appeared in the lateral occipital cortices, but not in V1 (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: 17.5% of the cortical volume preferentially activated by PF overlapped with the average spectroscopic VOI.
source: Bilaterally, 17.5% (i.e., 18 voxels out of 103) of the cortical volume preferentially activated by PF overlapped with the average spectroscopic VOI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), corresponding to a contamination of approximately 0.5% (i.e., 18 voxels out of 3691).
evidence: This is spatial analysis of fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average BOLD response in V1 (Brodmann Area 17) was similar for PF (0.85% ± 0.45%) and UF (0.80 ± 0.42%).
source: While the average BOLD response in V1 (Brodmann Area 17) was similar (0.85% ± 0.45% vs 0.80 ± 0.42%, paired sample t-test, p = 0.72) for the two stimulation conditions (Figure 1E), the average BOLD change in secondary visual areas (Brodmann Areas 18 and 19) was significantly (0.61% ± 0.29% vs 0.39 ± 0.18%, paired sample t-test, p = 0.008) higher during PF than UF (Figure 1F), indicating a larger output from V1 during PF compared with UF.
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The average BOLD change in secondary visual areas (Brodmann Areas 18 and 19) was significantly higher during PF (0.61% ± 0.29%) than UF (0.39 ± 0.18%).
source: While the average BOLD response in V1 (Brodmann Area 17) was similar (0.85% ± 0.45% vs 0.80 ± 0.42%, paired sample t-test, p = 0.72) for the two stimulation conditions (Figure 1E), the average BOLD change in secondary visual areas (Brodmann Areas 18 and 19) was significantly (0.61% ± 0.29% vs 0.39 ± 0.18%, paired sample t-test, p = 0.008) higher during PF than UF (Figure 1F), indicating a larger output from V1 during PF compared with UF.
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Higher BOLD change in secondary visual areas during PF compared to UF indicates a larger output from V1 during PF.
source: While the average BOLD response in V1 (Brodmann Area 17) was similar (0.85% ± 0.45% vs 0.80 ± 0.42%, paired sample t-test, p = 0.72) for the two stimulation conditions (Figure 1E), the average BOLD change in secondary visual areas (Brodmann Areas 18 and 19) was significantly (0.61% ± 0.29% vs 0.39 ± 0.18%, paired sample t-test, p = 0.008) higher during PF than UF (Figure 1F), indicating a larger output from V1 during PF compared with UF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known connectivity between V1 and secondary visual areas.

claim: V1 exhibited the same BOLD signal despite known differences in visual processing for PF and UF.
source: Thus, V1 exhibited the same BOLD signal despite known differences in visual processing for PF and UF (Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings, with reference to known differences in visual processing from cited literature.

claim: High quality (water linewidth 7.2 ± 0.6 Hz) and artifact-free spectra were reliably obtained from almost all subjects.
source: High quality (water linewidth 7.2 ± 0.6 Hz) and artifact-free spectra were reliably obtained from almost all subjects (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data quality information from the study, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Lactate concentration within V1 increased by 0.29 ± 0.18 μmol/g during the PF stimulation compared with resting conditions.
source: Compared with resting conditions, the lactate and glutamate concentrations within V1 increased by 0.29 ± 0.18 and 0.28 ± 0.16 μmol/g, respectively, during the PF stimulation corresponding to an increase of about 28% and 3%, respectively, over the baseline (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.001), whereas they both remained at their basal levels (−0.04 ± 0.13 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.42 for lactate, and 0.03 ± 0.17 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.63 for glutamate) during the UF stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lactate concentration increased by about 28% over baseline during PF stimulation.
source: Compared with resting conditions, the lactate and glutamate concentrations within V1 increased by 0.29 ± 0.18 and 0.28 ± 0.16 μmol/g, respectively, during the PF stimulation corresponding to an increase of about 28% and 3%, respectively, over the baseline (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.001), whereas they both remained at their basal levels (−0.04 ± 0.13 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.42 for lactate, and 0.03 ± 0.17 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.63 for glutamate) during the UF stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Glutamate concentration within V1 increased by 0.28 ± 0.16 μmol/g during the PF stimulation compared with resting conditions.
source: Compared with resting conditions, the lactate and glutamate concentrations within V1 increased by 0.29 ± 0.18 and 0.28 ± 0.16 μmol/g, respectively, during the PF stimulation corresponding to an increase of about 28% and 3%, respectively, over the baseline (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.001), whereas they both remained at their basal levels (−0.04 ± 0.13 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.42 for lactate, and 0.03 ± 0.17 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.63 for glutamate) during the UF stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Glutamate concentration increased by about 3% over baseline during PF stimulation.
source: Compared with resting conditions, the lactate and glutamate concentrations within V1 increased by 0.29 ± 0.18 and 0.28 ± 0.16 μmol/g, respectively, during the PF stimulation corresponding to an increase of about 28% and 3%, respectively, over the baseline (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.001), whereas they both remained at their basal levels (−0.04 ± 0.13 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.42 for lactate, and 0.03 ± 0.17 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.63 for glutamate) during the UF stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lactate and glutamate concentrations remained at their basal levels during the UF stimulation.
source: Compared with resting conditions, the lactate and glutamate concentrations within V1 increased by 0.29 ± 0.18 and 0.28 ± 0.16 μmol/g, respectively, during the PF stimulation corresponding to an increase of about 28% and 3%, respectively, over the baseline (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.001), whereas they both remained at their basal levels (−0.04 ± 0.13 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.42 for lactate, and 0.03 ± 0.17 μmol/g, qFDR = 0.63 for glutamate) during the UF stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lactate and glutamate responses were significantly different among the two stimulation conditions.
source: The lactate and glutamate responses were significantly different (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.01 for lactate and qFDR = 0.003 for glutamate) among the two stimulation conditions (Figure 3).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3.

claim: No other metabolites among those quantified showed a reliable stimulation-dependent change.
source: No other metabolites among those quantified showed a reliable stimulation-dependent change (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study.

claim: The study was unable to detect a reliable change for aspartate.
source: We were unable to detect a reliable change for aspartate (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.98), a proposed index of MAS and oxidative metabolism (Mangia et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study.

claim: Aspartate is a proposed index of MAS and oxidative metabolism.
source: We were unable to detect a reliable change for aspartate (paired sample t-test, qFDR = 0.98), a proposed index of MAS and oxidative metabolism (Mangia et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mangia et al., 2007a.

claim: There was a stimulation-induced decrease of tCr and tNAA linewidth during both PF and UF.
source: To confirm our fMRI result of similar BOLD effect during PF and UF, we examined linewidth narrowing of total creatine (tCr) and total N-acetylaspartate (tNAA) signals. We found a stimulation-induced decrease of tCr and tNAA linewidth during both PF and UF (Figure 3C, D) that was not statistically different between the two conditions (0.56 ± 0.04 vs 0.56 ± 0.05 Hz for tCr, paired sample t-test, p = 0.70; 0.55 ± 0.03 vs 0.56 ± 0.05 Hz for tNAA, paired sample t-test, p = 0.89).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The stimulation-induced decrease of tCr and tNAA linewidth was not statistically different between PF and UF conditions.
source: To confirm our fMRI result of similar BOLD effect during PF and UF, we examined linewidth narrowing of total creatine (tCr) and total N-acetylaspartate (tNAA) signals. We found a stimulation-induced decrease of tCr and tNAA linewidth during both PF and UF (Figure 3C, D) that was not statistically different between the two conditions (0.56 ± 0.04 vs 0.56 ± 0.05 Hz for tCr, paired sample t-test, p = 0.70; 0.55 ± 0.03 vs 0.56 ± 0.05 Hz for tNAA, paired sample t-test, p = 0.89).
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study, shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The difference between PF and rest spectra showed a signal in the region corresponding to lactate.
source: Specifically, the difference between PF and rest spectra showed a signal in the region corresponding to lactate, and in spectral regions corresponding to glutamate; both signals were absent in the difference between UF and rest spectra.
evidence: This is analysis of 1H-fMRS difference spectra from the study.

claim: The difference between PF and rest spectra showed signals in spectral regions corresponding to glutamate.
source: Specifically, the difference between PF and rest spectra showed a signal in the region corresponding to lactate, and in spectral regions corresponding to glutamate; both signals were absent in the difference between UF and rest spectra.
evidence: This is analysis of 1H-fMRS difference spectra from the study.

claim: Lactate and glutamate signals were absent in the difference between UF and rest spectra.
source: Specifically, the difference between PF and rest spectra showed a signal in the region corresponding to lactate, and in spectral regions corresponding to glutamate; both signals were absent in the difference between UF and rest spectra.
evidence: This is analysis of 1H-fMRS difference spectra from the study.

claim: The only correlated signals that survived in the difference spectrum between PF and UF were lactate and glutamate.
source: Overall, the only correlated signals that survived in the difference spectrum between PF and UF were lactate and glutamate, which strongly supports the significance of the concentration changes based on LCModel quantifications.
evidence: This is analysis of 1H-fMRS difference spectra from the study.

claim: The cortical gray matter of the brain features one of the highest metabolic rates of all organ tissues of the human body.
source: The cortical gray matter of the brain features one of the highest metabolic rates of all organ tissues of the human body.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Energy is a limiting factor for the human cerebral cortex.
source: Although energy is recognized as a limiting factor for the human cerebral cortex (Herculano-Houzel, 2011; Niven and Laughlin, 2008), the increase in lactate concentration occurring upon sensory stimulation is not the result of limited oxygen availability (Aalling et al., 2018; DiNuzzo, 2016), as it is for skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herculano-Houzel, 2011 and Niven and Laughlin, 2008.

claim: The increase in lactate concentration occurring upon sensory stimulation is not the result of limited oxygen availability.
source: Although energy is recognized as a limiting factor for the human cerebral cortex (Herculano-Houzel, 2011; Niven and Laughlin, 2008), the increase in lactate concentration occurring upon sensory stimulation is not the result of limited oxygen availability (Aalling et al., 2018; DiNuzzo, 2016), as it is for skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aalling et al., 2018 and DiNuzzo, 2016.

claim: Glycolysis serves specific neurophysiological and neurobiological purposes, such as axonal vesicle transport, vesicle recycling, action potential waveform modulation, reuptake of neuroactive compounds, and dendritic spine remodeling.
source: Why the cerebral cortex upregulates glycolytic metabolism for sensory information processing is unknown, but it is well established that glycolysis serves specific neurophysiological and neurobiological purposes, such as axonal vesicle transport, vesicle recycling, action potential waveform modulation, reuptake of neuroactive compounds, and dendritic spine remodeling (reviewed in DiNuzzo and Nedergaard, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review by DiNuzzo and Nedergaard, 2017.

claim: Lactate is implicated in cognitive processes occurring during waking activity, like learning and memory.
source: Furthermore, lactate is known to be implicated in cognitive processes occurring during waking activity, like learning and memory (Descalzi et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2011; Scavuzzo et al., 2020; Suzuki et al., 2011), although the exact underlying mechanisms are still debated (Dienel, 2019b; Steinman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The exact mechanisms by which lactate is implicated in learning and memory are still debated.
source: Furthermore, lactate is known to be implicated in cognitive processes occurring during waking activity, like learning and memory (Descalzi et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2011; Scavuzzo et al., 2020; Suzuki et al., 2011), although the exact underlying mechanisms are still debated (Dienel, 2019b; Steinman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dienel, 2019b and Steinman et al., 2016.

claim: Stimulus perception affects the lactate and glutamate response in V1.
source: In the present study, we asked whether alterations in visual perception are also reflected in metabolic changes within the primary visual cortex in humans. We report that stimulus perception affects the lactate and glutamate response in V1.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by 1H-fMRS data.

claim: The PF and UF stimulations elicited the same average BOLD signals increase inside V1, indicating an equivalent degree of neurovascular coupling in the two experimental conditions.
source: The PF and UF stimulations elicited, by experimental design, the same average BOLD signals increase inside V1, indicating an equivalent degree of neurovascular coupling and possibly of local synaptic activity in the two experimental conditions (Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: This is based on fMRI data and supported by citation to Logothetis, 2008.

claim: The same average BOLD signals increase inside V1 during PF and UF possibly indicates equivalent local synaptic activity in the two experimental conditions.
source: The PF and UF stimulations elicited, by experimental design, the same average BOLD signals increase inside V1, indicating an equivalent degree of neurovascular coupling and possibly of local synaptic activity in the two experimental conditions (Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on fMRI data and supported by citation to Logothetis, 2008.

claim: A significant increase in the regional lactate level occurred only during the PF stimulus, with no appreciable change of lactate during the UF stimulus compared with resting conditions.
source: Yet, we observed a significant increase in the regional lactate level only during the PF stimulus, with no appreciable change of lactate during the UF stimulus compared with resting conditions.
evidence: This is 1H-fMRS data from the study.

claim: A temporal dissociation between BOLD and lactate changes has been previously reported during repeated photic stimulations.
source: A temporal dissociation between BOLD and lactate changes has been previously reported during repeated photic stimulations (Mangia et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mangia et al., 2007b.

claim: During repeated photic stimulations, BOLD response was preserved, but not the lactate accumulation, possibly due to habituation of neuronal firing.
source: In that case, BOLD response was preserved, but not the lactate accumulation, possibly due to habituation of neuronal firing.
evidence: This is based on cited literature and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Metabolic adaptation, in terms of glutamate levels, in the presence of constant BOLD and electrophysiological activity was reported in epilepsy.
source: Metabolic adaptation, in terms of glutamate levels, in the presence of constant BOLD and electrophysiological activity was also reported in epilepsy (Peca et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peca et al., 2010.

claim: The physiological mechanisms underlying BOLD signals and energy metabolism do not necessarily overlap under all experimental conditions.
source: These results suggest that the physiological mechanisms underlying BOLD signals and energy metabolism do not necessarily overlap under all experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited literature and the current study's findings.

claim: Lactate and glutamate may be dissociated from BOLD changes when cortical input and output are differentially modulated by intracortical or thalamocortical inhibition.
source: Our results suggest that lactate and glutamate may be dissociated from BOLD changes when cortical input and output are differentially modulated by for example, intracortical (Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007) or thalamocortical (Min et al., 2020) inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: An overall switch toward inhibition is expected to reduce the energy request of the brain, thus impacting on metabolic rates independently of BOLD response.
source: In fact, an overall switch toward inhibition is expected to reduce the energy request of the brain, thus impacting on metabolic rates independently of BOLD response (Mangia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mangia et al., 2009.

claim: Inhibition, in terms of GABA concentration, has been positively correlated with changes of the BOLD signal.
source: Although inhibition, in terms of GABA concentration, has been positively correlated with changes of the BOLD signal (Chen et al., 2005; Donahue et al., 2014; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2009; Northoff et al., 2007), the dependence of GABAergic neurotransmission and corresponding BOLD changes upon temporal flickering frequency is difficult to predict, as the gating of sensory information is much likely supported by dishinibitory mechanisms (e.g., through vasoactive intestinal peptide-positive interneurons) (Askew et al., 2019; Gasselin et al., 2021; Pi et al., 2013; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The gating of sensory information is likely supported by disinhibitory mechanisms (e.g., through vasoactive intestinal peptide-positive interneurons).
source: Although inhibition, in terms of GABA concentration, has been positively correlated with changes of the BOLD signal (Chen et al., 2005; Donahue et al., 2014; Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2009; Northoff et al., 2007), the dependence of GABAergic neurotransmission and corresponding BOLD changes upon temporal flickering frequency is difficult to predict, as the gating of sensory information is much likely supported by dishinibitory mechanisms (e.g., through vasoactive intestinal peptide-positive interneurons) (Askew et al., 2019; Gasselin et al., 2021; Pi et al., 2013; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Changes in excitation/inhibition equilibrium have been proposed as a source of variability of the CBF/CMRO2 coupling ratio.
source: Accordingly, changes in excitation/inhibition equilibrium have been proposed as a source of variability of the CBF/CMRO2 coupling ratio (Buxton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buxton et al., 2014.

claim: The metabolic response is capable of differentiating neural states that are intrinsically distinct, although they induce the same BOLD response.
source: In more general terms, the metabolic response seems capable of differentiating neural states that are intrinsically distinct, although they induce the same BOLD response (Moradi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moradi et al., 2012.

claim: The firing rate of layer IV neurons that receive input from LGN is higher during UF than PF.
source: In particular, the firing rate of layer IV neurons that receive input from LGN is higher during UF than PF, as evidenced by the synchronization of these neurons to the stimulus frequency (Gur and Snodderly, 1997; Herrmann, 2001; Norcia et al., 2015; Pastor et al., 2003; Regan, 1989; Vialatte et al., 2010), yet we found that lactate and glutamate increases during PF, not UF.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The stimulation-induced effect on metabolite concentrations is happening downstream of the input stage in layer IV, and specifically during the intracortical processing involving output layers II/III and V.
source: These findings indicate that the stimulation-induced effect on metabolite concentrations is happening downstream of the input stage in layer IV, and specifically during the intracortical processing involving output layers II/III and V.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation between layer IV firing rates and metabolic changes.

claim: High-frequency flickering (30–60 Hz) abolished MUA, a measure of neuronal spiking (putatively from layer II/III), but not single neuron recordings from layer IV.
source: This conclusion is supported by the fact that high-frequency flickering (30–60 Hz) abolished MUA, a measure of neuronal spiking (putatively from layer II/III) (Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007), but not single neuron recordings from layer IV (Gur and Snodderly, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007 and Gur and Snodderly, 1997.

claim: The observed outcome can be explained by distinct signaling mechanisms underlying spiking and synaptic activity that are frequency dependent.
source: Using compartmentalized metabolic modeling, we have recently obtained evidence that the abovementioned outcome can be explained by distinct signaling mechanisms underlying spiking and synaptic activity (e.g., pre- and postsynaptic ionic currents) that are indeed frequency dependent (DiNuzzo and Giove, 2012; DiNuzzo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous modeling work, supported by citations.

claim: Chromatic and achromatic flickering at the same temporal frequency elicited the same neurochemical response in V1 despite differences in the responding neuronal populations (i.e., blob vs interblob).
source: We previously reported that chromatic and achromatic flickering at the same temporal frequency elicited the same neurochemical response in V1 despite differences in the responding neuronal populations (i.e., blob vs interblob) (Bednařík et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Lactate and glutamate, and hence aerobic glycolysis, are sensitive to cortical processing (e.g., input/output or excitation/inhibition balance) rather than the targeted neuronal population.
source: Together with the results that we report here, this observation suggests that lactate and glutamate, and hence aerobic glycolysis, are both sensitive to cortical processing (e.g., input/output or excitation/inhibition balance) rather than the targeted neuronal population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings and previous work.

claim: Increased glutamate levels reflect an upregulation of the MAS.
source: Our results can be interpreted in keeping with the concept that increased glutamate levels reflect an upregulation of the MAS (Mangia et al., 2012), although we were unable to report significant differences in aspartate levels likely due to insufficient sensitivity of MRS at 3T.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mangia et al., 2012.

claim: The decrease in aspartate during sensory stimulation is commonly observed at 7T, but has never been reported at 3T, most likely due to limited sensitivity of detection.
source: Indeed, the decrease in aspartate during sensory stimulation is commonly observed at 7T, but to our knowledge has never been reported at 3T, most likely due to limited sensitivity of detection.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The NADH produced by the metabolism of glucose to lactate has to be transported from the cytosol to the mitochondria to be used for energy production within the electron transport chain.
source: The NADH produced by the metabolism of glucose to lactate has to be transported from the cytosol to the mitochondria to be used for energy production within the electron transport chain.
evidence: This is established metabolic knowledge.

claim: The MAS requires that glutamate is transported from cytosol to mitochondria and concomitantly aspartate is counter-transported from mitochondria to cytosol through the aspartate–glutamate carrier (AGC1/Aralar).
source: Among other components of the MAS, such process requires that glutamate is transported from cytosol to mitochondria and concomitantly aspartate is counter-transported from mitochondria to cytosol through the aspartate–glutamate carrier (AGC1/Aralar).
evidence: This is established metabolic knowledge.

claim: The AGC1/Aralar carrier-mediated transport is a rate-limiting step within the MAS.
source: The AGC1/Aralar carrier-mediated transport is a rate-limiting step within the MAS and therefore it lags behind the concomitant increase in tricarboxylic acids cycle and NAD+/NADH-redox shuttling in mitochondria.
evidence: This is established metabolic knowledge.

claim: The increase in glutamate (and decrease in aspartate) concentration reflects an increase in the rate of MAS, with accumulation of glutamate at the cytosolic side and reduction of aspartate at the mitochondrial side.
source: In agreement with existing literature (Hertz and Chen, 2017a; Hertz and Rothman, 2017b; Lin et al., 2012; Mangia et al., 2012; Mangia et al., 2007a), we interpret the increase in glutamate (and decrease in aspartate) concentration as reflecting an increase in the rate of MAS, with accumulation of glutamate at the cytosolic side and reduction of aspartate at the mitochondrial side.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The MAS does not necessarily correlate with mitochondrial respiration and cerebral blood flow.
source: Notably, the MAS does not necessarily correlate with mitochondrial respiration and cerebral blood flow, as evidenced by the findings that (1) oxidative metabolism and CMRO2 are enhanced at both low and high flickering frequencies (Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007), and (2) glutamate and aspartate, but not lactate, correlate with BOLD signals during low frequency (~8 Hz) visual stimulation (Bednařík et al., 2018; Ip et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The increase in lactate and glutamate levels is the consequence of the surge in glycolysis and the ensuing increase of cytosolic NADH:NAD+ ratio taking place during neuronal activation.
source: To what extent aerobic glycolysis and MAS can dissociate from oxidative phosphorylation in the brain remains to be established, but previously published data strongly indicate that the increase in lactate and glutamate levels is the consequence of the surge in glycolysis and the ensuing increase of cytosolic NADH:NAD+ ratio taking place during neuronal activation (Díaz-García et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Díaz-García et al., 2017.

claim: Secondary visual areas were recruited to a larger extent during PF stimulus than UF stimulus.
source: While the similar BOLD response in V1 is a direct consequence of our experimental design, we additionally found that secondary visual areas were recruited to a larger extent during PF stimulus than UF stimulus, supporting the argument that their activation is necessary for perception (Lamme et al., 2000; Salminen-Vaparanta et al., 2019; Tong, 2003).
evidence: This is fMRI data from the study, and the interpretation is supported by citations.

claim: The activation of secondary visual areas is necessary for perception.
source: While the similar BOLD response in V1 is a direct consequence of our experimental design, we additionally found that secondary visual areas were recruited to a larger extent during PF stimulus than UF stimulus, supporting the argument that their activation is necessary for perception (Lamme et al., 2000; Salminen-Vaparanta et al., 2019; Tong, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamme et al., 2000, Salminen-Vaparanta et al., 2019, and Tong, 2003.

claim: The preferential response of secondary visual areas to perceived stimuli confirms previous results of strong BOLD activity in ventral and dorsal streams during visible stimuli and a reduction of their activity in conditions of invisible stimulation.
source: The preferential response of secondary visual areas to perceived stimuli that we observe here broadly confirms previous results of a strong BOLD activity in ventral ('visual-for-perception' processing) and dorsal ('visual-for-action' processing) streams during visible stimuli and a reduction of their activity in conditions of invisible stimulation (Hesselmann and Malach, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hesselmann and Malach, 2011.

claim: The higher activation of secondary visual areas cannot be conclusively and unambiguously established to be causally linked to perception.
source: However, since our stimulation protocol is associated by design with higher activation of output layers of V1 and hence higher input to V2/V3, we cannot conclusively and unambiguously establish that the higher activation of secondary visual areas is causally linked to perception.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on their experimental design.

claim: The role of the primary visual cortex in stimulus perception is an intense area of research.
source: The role of the primary visual cortex in stimulus perception is an intense area of research (Gail et al., 2004; Leopold and Logothetis, 1996; Maier et al., 2008; Polonsky et al., 2000; Wunderlich et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous fMRI studies investigating the dependence of V1 BOLD activity on visual perception produced controversial results.
source: Previous fMRI studies investigating the dependence of V1 BOLD activity on visual perception produced controversial results, which might be related to the difficulty of disentangling perception from spatial attention.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Attention, but not perception, modulates the BOLD signal in human V1.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that attention, but not perception, modulates the BOLD signal in human V1 (Watanabe et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2011.

claim: Perception was found to enhance the BOLD response within V1 for specific experimental designs (e.g., flash suppression of perception).
source: In fact, perception was found to enhance the BOLD response within V1 for specific experimental designs (e.g., flash suppression of perception) (Yuval-Greenberg and Heeger, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yuval-Greenberg and Heeger, 2013.

claim: The study employed a stimulation paradigm that allowed inducing the same BOLD response within V1 under the two experimental conditions by adjusting the stimulation contrast.
source: Our study employed a substantially different stimulation paradigm that specifically allowed us, by adjusting the stimulation contrast, to induce the same BOLD response, and inductively an equivalent mean degree of synaptic activity, within V1 under the two experimental conditions (Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, supported by citation.

claim: The study did not use any additional stimulus (e.g., visual masking) to suppress or modulate visual perception.
source: Most importantly, we did not use any additional stimulus (e.g., visual masking) to suppress or modulate visual perception.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The study used a simple way to modulate perception for extended periods of time (required by 1H-fMRS) while maintaining attention at a nearly constant level.
source: On the contrary, we used a simple way to modulate perception for extended periods of time (required by 1H-fMRS) while maintaining attention at a nearly constant level, as evidenced by pupillometry and task performance.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, supported by behavioral and physiological data.

claim: The BOLD response in V1 to flickering at full-contrast peaks at 4–8 Hz and settles around 70% of its maximal value even at frequencies above 30 Hz.
source: In particular, we employed the well-known dependence of BOLD response in V1 to flickering, which at full-contrast peaks at 4–8 Hz and settles around 70% of its maximal value even at frequencies above 30 Hz (Thomas and Menon, 1998), that is, in the absence of flickering perception.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thomas and Menon, 1998.

claim: The peak activations in V1 and secondary visual areas are stimulation dependent and occur at distinct temporal frequencies.
source: Previous literature reported that the peak activations in V1 and secondary visual areas are stimulation dependent and occur at distinct temporal frequencies (4 or 8 Hz in V1, and 20 or 40 Hz in secondary visual areas for chromatic or luminance flickering, respectively) (Chai et al., 2019; Fox et al., 1986; Kastner et al., 2004; Kwong et al., 1992; Singh et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The preferred frequency of secondary visual areas is just below the CFF for chromatic flickering (~25 Hz) and luminance flickering (~50 Hz).
source: Interestingly, the preferred frequency of secondary visual areas is just below the CFF for chromatic flickering (~25 Hz) and luminance flickering (~50 Hz) (Shady et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shady et al., 2004.

claim: The isoluminant chromatic flickering stimulation at 30 Hz is above the CFF.
source: In our experiments, the isoluminant chromatic flickering stimulation at 30 Hz is above the CFF and accordingly we found that the BOLD response in secondary visual areas drops substantially compared with the concurrent BOLD response in V1.
evidence: This is based on the experimental design and fMRI data.

claim: By using visual stimulations below and above the CFF and adjusting the contrast of the low-frequency stimulus, the study was able to modulate perception alongside BOLD activity in secondary visual areas with unchanged BOLD activity in V1.
source: Overall, by using visual stimulations below and above the CFF and adjusting the contrast of the low-frequency stimulus we were able to modulate perception alongside BOLD activity in secondary visual areas with a unchanged BOLD activity in V1.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental design and its outcomes.

claim: Subtle differences in the qualitative nature of the BOLD signal response might exist between the two conditions, although the trends toward longer onset time and time-to-peak during UF compared with PF were not statistically significant.
source: It should be noted that subtle differences in the qualitative nature of the BOLD signal response might exist between the two conditions, although the trends toward longer onset time and time-to-peak during UF compared with PF were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Long acquisition times are required for achieving a good sensitivity of the 1H-fMRS measurements and a reliable metabolite quantification, even at magnetic fields of 3T.
source: For instance, the fMRI measurements have been obtained using 30 s epochs, while the fMRS measurements have been obtained using 4 min epochs. Long acquisition times are required for achieving a good sensitivity of the 1H-fMRS measurements and a reliable metabolite quantification, even at magnetic fields of 3T.
evidence: This is a technical limitation of the 1H-fMRS method.

claim: Prolonged (i.e., minutes) stimulations elicit a persistent BOLD response with minimal attenuation in both humans and rats.
source: Nonetheless, results in both humans (Mangia et al., 2007b) and rats (Just et al., 2013) have shown that prolonged (i.e., minutes) stimulations elicit a persistent BOLD response with minimal attenuation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mangia et al., 2007b and Just et al., 2013.

claim: The BOLD effect during the fMRS acquisition was relatively stable as determined by the linewidth changes of tCr and tNAA signals.
source: Although we cannot exclude a certain degree of neuronal adaptation, we confirmed that the BOLD effect during the fMRS acquisition was indeed relatively stable as determined by the linewidth changes of tCr and tNAA signals.
evidence: This is based on 1H-fMRS data analysis.

claim: The observed changes in lactate levels might include distinct neuronal populations showing nonuniform responses due to the large volume used for 1H-fMRS measurements.
source: Another limitation to consider is represented by the large volume used for 1H-fMRS measurements. It could be possible that the observed changes in lactate levels include distinct neuronal populations showing nonuniform responses.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Heterogeneity in the response to stimulation within V1 might be due to eccentricity.
source: Indeed, although the main differential effect of frequency was located far from the calcarine sulcus, it also involved some mid hemispheric areas presumably included in the spectroscopic voxel. As an illustration, heterogeneity in the response to stimulation within V1 might be due to, for example, eccentricity (Chai et al., 2019), which we however minimized by using a 3° foveal stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chai et al., 2019.

claim: There is hemispheric lateralization for the spatial frequencies.
source: There is also an hemispheric lateralization for the spatial frequencies (Kauffmann et al., 2014), but this is not likely to apply to our study, as we used the same radial checkerboard (i.e., including many spatial frequencies) for both PF and UF.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kauffmann et al., 2014.

claim: The changes in BOLD signal during PF and UF were nearly double in the anatomical V1 compared with the spectroscopic VOI, indicating a substantial partial-volume effect.
source: The finding that the changes in BOLD signal during PF and UF were nearly double in the anatomical (i.e., Brodmann atlas-based) V1 compared with the spectroscopic VOI indicates a substantial partial-volume effect.
evidence: This is based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: The lactate concentration change reported in the study might be underestimated due to partial-volume effects.
source: The associated loss of sensitivity entails that the lactate concentration change that we report here might in fact be underestimated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial-volume effect.

claim: Feedback input to V1 from secondary visual areas might be taking place during stimulus perception.
source: Furthermore, we cannot exclude that feedback input to V1 from secondary visual areas might be taking place during stimulus perception (Watkins et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watkins et al., 2006.

claim: Under the experimental design, the BOLD activity in V1 largely reflected stimulus features.
source: However, under our experimental design we were able to fully control BOLD response in V1 by only acting on stimulus contrast, without altering the subjective perception of the stimuli, which indicates that the BOLD activity in V1 largely reflected stimulus features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The study based the positioning of the spectroscopic VOI solely on the online estimate of the stimulus-induced BOLD signal change.
source: Finally, we based the positioning of the spectroscopic VOI solely on the online estimate of the stimulus-induced BOLD signal change.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The study could not perform online retinotopic mapping for driving the positioning of the spectroscopic VOI, as this would have increased the acquisition protocol duration to an impractical length.
source: In particular, we could not perform online retinotopic mapping for driving the positioning of the spectroscopic VOI, as this would have increased the acquisition protocol duration to an impractical length for guaranteeing good attention levels and absence of motion during the 1H-fMRS session.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Partial-volume effects are unavoidable because the STEAM sequence requires a box-shaped VOI.
source: In any case, partial-volume effects are unavoidable because the STEAM sequence we used requires a box-shaped VOI, which would have not allowed us to entirely avoid the inclusion of tissue outside V1, regardless of the availability of the retinotopic map.
evidence: This is a technical limitation of the 1H-fMRS method.

claim: Visual perception has a measurable metabolic effect on V1.
source: In this study, we report for the first time that visual perception has a measurable metabolic effect on V1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by 1H-fMRS data.

claim: The study could not establish any causal relation between metabolism and perception.
source: Although we could not establish any causal relation between metabolism and perception, our findings imply that BOLD-fMRI and 1H-fMRS are complementary techniques.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: BOLD-fMRI and 1H-fMRS are complementary techniques capable of highlighting different aspects of neural activation and stimulus processing.
source: Although we could not establish any causal relation between metabolism and perception, our findings imply that BOLD-fMRI and 1H-fMRS are complementary techniques. Specifically, they are capable of highlighting different aspects of neural activation and stimulus processing, for example, under conditions in which synaptic and spiking activity are partially disentangled due to an alteration of excitation/inhibition patterns and, in turn, local input/output balance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The results can be translated to other sensory modalities.
source: Although we focused on the visual pathways, it is conceivable that our results can be translated to other sensory modalities.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the generalizability of their findings.

claim: Tactile or auditory stimulations during vegetative state can still activate primary somatosensory cortex (S1) or primary auditory cortex (A1), respectively, in the absence of perception and without the involvement of higher-order associative areas.
source: For example, tactile (Laureys et al., 2002) or auditory (Boly et al., 2004; Laureys et al., 2000) stimulations during vegetative state can still activate primary somatosensory cortex (S1) or primary auditory cortex (A1), respectively, in the absence of perception and without the involvement of higher-order associative areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laureys et al., 2002, Boly et al., 2004, and Laureys et al., 2000.

claim: The cortical metabolic profile might be an indicator of sensory perception.
source: We suggest that the cortical metabolic profile might be an indicator of sensory perception, in keeping with the dynamics of lactate and glutamate across the sleep–wake cycle (Aalling et al., 2018; DiNuzzo and Nedergaard, 2017; Naylor et al., 2012; Naylor et al., 2011) as well as with the relation between lactate and arousal (Zuend et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Elevated brain lactate and glutamate levels are associated with wakefulness and memory formation.
source: Elevated brain lactate and glutamate levels are associated with wakefulness and memory formation, which naturally require the processing of incoming sensory stimuli, like the control exerted by the central visual pathways for either gating or filtering out behaviorally relevant or irrelevant visual information.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: The metabolic responses to perceived, but not unperceived, sensory stimulation could be enabling factors for learning and memory.
source: As such, the metabolic responses to perceived, but not unperceived, sensory stimulation could be enabling factors for learning and memory, as indicated by the relevance of aerobic glycolysis and lactate in synaptic plasticity mechanisms (Bueschke et al., 2021; Descalzi et al., 2019; DiNuzzo, 2016; Harris et al., 2019; Herrera-López et al., 2020; Jourdain et al., 2018; Kobayashi et al., 2019; Lundquist et al., 2021; Margineanu et al., 2018; Scavuzzo et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis and lactate are relevant in synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
source: As such, the metabolic responses to perceived, but not unperceived, sensory stimulation could be enabling factors for learning and memory, as indicated by the relevance of aerobic glycolysis and lactate in synaptic plasticity mechanisms (Bueschke et al., 2021; Descalzi et al., 2019; DiNuzzo, 2016; Harris et al., 2019; Herrera-López et al., 2020; Jourdain et al., 2018; Kobayashi et al., 2019; Lundquist et al., 2021; Margineanu et al., 2018; Scavuzzo et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis and lactate might reflect cortical information processing and intracortical communication.
source: In particular, aerobic glycolysis and lactate might reflect cortical information processing and, in turn, intracortical communication, in agreement with the relation between regional metabolic rates of glucose utilization and resting-state network dynamics in the cerebral cortex (Jamadar et al., 2020; Noack et al., 2017; Spetsieris et al., 2015; Su et al., 2018; Thompson, 2018).
evidence: This is speculation by the authors, supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a relation between regional metabolic rates of glucose utilization and resting-state network dynamics in the cerebral cortex.
source: In particular, aerobic glycolysis and lactate might reflect cortical information processing and, in turn, intracortical communication, in agreement with the relation between regional metabolic rates of glucose utilization and resting-state network dynamics in the cerebral cortex (Jamadar et al., 2020; Noack et al., 2017; Spetsieris et al., 2015; Su et al., 2018; Thompson, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.
